title: Adaptive speculative handshake: kernel-aware backpressure, dynamic acceptance curves, and circuit-breaker fallback
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background:
We run dual-path speculative decode in the runtime: a fast lightweight model tries to produce early tokens while a heavyweight model computes full-quality output. Current routing uses static acceptance thresholds and simple prefills which cause two problems at scale: (1) kernel mismatch leads to hotspots because some model variants trigger slow attention kernels, and (2) under sustained load the early-path produces spurious accepts or false negatives, causing waste or increased tail latency.

Goal:
Design and implement an adaptive speculative handshake that: (a) is kernel-aware (routes probes and commits considering kernel fingerprint & current kernel queueing), (b) applies dynamic acceptance curves that adapt to observed per-route precision/recall and latency distribution, and (c) includes a circuit-breaker style fallback to fall back to single-path decode under degraded conditions. The end-state should reduce wasted tokens and keep P99 latency within SLOs while preserving end-user output quality.

Non-goals:
- Replacing model selection policies (we'll integrate with model catalog separately).
- Full multi-tenancy scheduler redesign (scope limited to handshake + routing heuristics).

Proposal (high level):
1) Kernel fingerprinting and scoring:
   - Extend the runtime telemetry to emit a compact kernel fingerprint per candidate model variant (attention type, quantization path, expected kernel latency bucket).
   - Maintain an in-memory short-term kernel congestion score (exponential decay) per kernel fingerprint.
   - Router uses kernel score + capacity headroom to prioritize probe dispatch to compatible hardware/kernels.

2) Dynamic acceptance curves:
   - Replace static threshold with a per-route sigmoid acceptance curve parameterized by: precision target, latency budget, and recent acceptance precision/false accept rate.
   - Continuously update curve parameters via lightweight online calibration: when a probe's tentative output gets validated by final model, update precision estimate and shift curve to maintain target precision within latency budget.
   - Persist curve parameters per route/model-version for warm starts.

3) Circuit-breaker fallback:
   - Three triggers to engage fallback: kernel congestion > K, acceptance false-positive rate > F over window W, or tail latency drift P99 > SLO_margin.
   - Fallback mode: stop speculative early-commits for affected route/model and bias routing towards single-path decode. Provide an auto-recovery window with gradually reintroducing probes via canary sampling.

Operational acceptance metrics (must be instrumented):
- End-to-end P50/P95/P99 inference latency per route (baseline vs speculative on/off).
- Speculative wasted token rate: tokens generated by early-path not used in final output / total tokens produced.
- Acceptance precision & recall: fraction of early commits that match final tokens (top-k match heuristics) and proportion of final tokens missed by early path.
- Kernel congestion score distribution and correlation with P99.
- Cost delta (estimated token-GPU-seconds) for active speculative vs single-path.

Performance targets:
- Reduce wasted token rate by >= 35% on routes with historically high false accepts while keeping P99 <= baseline_P99 + 10ms (soft target).
- When fallback active, overall system must keep 95% of routes within SLOs.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Complexity vs gains: dynamic curves require additional telemetry and state; mitigated by keeping calibration window short and per-route defaults.
- Aggressive fallbacks reduce wasted work but may increase average latency for some users; the canary reintroduction policy aims to recover cheaply.
- Kernel-aware routing could route probes to a suboptimal model instance if not careful; we'll prioritize kernel compatibility over absolute throughput for probes only.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- M1 (2w): Telemetry extension: kernel fingerprint & kernel congestion score emitter + storage. (ENG owners: Marco, Lina)
- M2 (2w): Router changes: incorporate kernel score into probe dispatch decision + simple backpressure guard.
- M3 (2w): Acceptance curve framework + online calibrator (simulator mode behind flag).
- M4 (2w): Circuit-breaker state machine + canary reintroduction + admin controls in Console.
- M5 (2w): Integration tests, perf benchmarks, staged rollout to Dedicated region Canary.

Testing & rollout strategy:
- Start in feature-flagged simulator: replay historical traces and measure acceptance precision and wasted tokens.
- Canary rollout on internal staging cluster with 1% of traffic. Collect telemetry for 48–72h, validate metrics.
- Phased ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% with rollback criteria defined (P99 spike > 2x, wasted token rate increase > 20% relative to baseline).

Runbook & operator controls:
- Console toggle per-tenant and per-route to disable speculative handshake.
- Emergency off-switch: global feature flag to disable all probes.
- Circuit-breaker exposes state in Console with suggested actions (increase thresholds, drain kernels).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Precise kernel fingerprint fields to include (suggest: attention-type, kv-cache-mode, quantized-precision, fused-kernel-id).
- Acceptance matching heuristics: exact token match vs embedding-similarity for paraphrase-tolerant routes.
- Cost accounting: how to attribute wasted token cost to tenant vs system.

Related artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Adaptive+Speculative+Handshake
- Simulation harness PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4218
- Initial perf run (internal dashboard): https://dash.redwood.ai/d/handshake/2026-02-28

Deliverables:
- Runtime: kernel telemetry, router changes, acceptance calibrator, circuit-breaker state machine.
- Console: route-level controls and visibility, recovery/actions UI.
- Tests: replay harness scenarios, integration perf suite, canary monitoring dashboards.

Success criteria (post-launch):
- Wasted token rate down >= 25% across top 50 routes within 2 weeks.
- No more than 5% of routes experience P99 degradation > 10ms attributable to this change.
- Operators report improved visibility and fewer manual fallbacks.

If approved, start with M1 immediately.
